newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH PENSION REFORM BILLS SEEN READY IN Q1 1997.
newsitem.headline: POLISH PENSION REFORM BILLS SEEN READY IN Q1 1997.

text.p: Polish Labour Minister Andrzej Baczkowski said on Wednesday he would prepare bills triggering the crucial reform of the country's inefficient social security system by the end of March next year.

The four bills, which parliament should adopt by the end of 1997, will include two pivotal ones -- on the creation of new privately managed pension funds and endowing them with shares of firms undergoing privatisation, he told a news conference.
"If we fail to launch the reform quickly, our social security system will collapse ... in the next century, and an economic catastrophe will follow," Baczkowski said.

Poland's current social security system, inherited from the communist era before 1989, poses a serious threat to public finances with the number pensioners expected to rise from the current of nine million to 11 million in the year 2010.
Pensions cost the national budget more than 20 percent of its revenues annually and the share could steeply rise unless the reform is implemented, Baczkowski said.

After the reform, each Pole would receive his pension from three sources rather than only from the state-owned Social Security Office (ZUS), which collects from employers 45 percent of workers' wages and immediately spends the cash on pensions.
The first, and at first the biggest, part of a person's pension would still come from ZUS, whose operations will however be rationalised.

As of 1998 ZUS would start monitoring each worker's contribution and base his or her future pension on the size of premiums and duration of employment, replacing the current complicated system of calculating pensions, Baczkowski said.
The second part of the pension would come from new, privately managed pension funds, to be set up in the next several years.
The funds, under close government supervision, will mandatorily receive part of the premium now paid to ZUS and invest their capital in safe securities.

Baczkowski said that people now in schools and maybe also young workers would be obliged to pay premiums to the funds while older workers, but below 50 years of age, would be free to chose whether to join the funds or rely only on ZUS.
He said the funds' capital would be strengthened with shares of privatised companies but did not give any details.
The government earlier said the funds were likely to get minority stakes of companies with good financial results, such as the telecommunications giant TPSA, distilleries and banks.
Private-owned funds and insurance companies would be the third source of the pension and the government would offer tax relief to people saving in them, Baczkowski said.
He also confirmed that the retirement age for women would not be increased to 65 from the current 60 as earlier planned.
The first bill under the social security reform is already in parliament. It curbs annual pension rises by pegging them to a special basket of consumer goods prices.
